note: Curated from the sources listed per entry. Amounts are typical amounts used in studies or on labels, shown for information only, never as a prescription.

supplements.name: Whey protein
supplements.summary: A milk protein powder that makes it easier to reach a daily protein target.
supplements.typical_dose: One scoop (about 25 to 30 g powder, 20 to 25 g protein)
supplements.timing: Any time of day; many people take it after training or with a meal.
cautions: Contains milk protein; not for people with a milk allergy. Whey isolate has very little lactose.
Food first: protein powder only fills a gap your meals don't cover.
Choose products that list protein per serving and have FSSAI approval.

sources.title: ISSN position stand: protein and exercise (Jäger et al., 2017)
NIH ODS: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance
FSSAI Health Supplements and Nutraceuticals Regulations, 2022

supplements.name: Plant protein
supplements.summary: Pea, soy or rice protein powder; a dairy-free way to add protein.
supplements.typical_dose: One scoop (about 30 to 35 g powder, 20 to 25 g protein)
supplements.timing: Any time of day; many people take it after training or with a meal.
cautions: Blends of pea and rice give a more complete set of amino acids than one source alone.
Soy-based powders aren't suitable with a soy allergy.

sources.title: ISSN position stand: protein and exercise (Jäger et al., 2017)
NIH ODS: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance

supplements.name: Creatine monohydrate
supplements.summary: One of the most studied supplements for strength and short, intense effort.

evidence.use: Strength and power with resistance training

supplements.timing: Any time of day, every day; timing matters less than taking it consistently.
cautions: Can add 1 to 2 kg of water weight in the first weeks; this isn't fat.
Creatine raises blood creatinine a little, which can make kidney tests look worse. Tell your doctor you take it.
Not advised with kidney disease unless your doctor agrees.
interactions: Medicines that affect the kidneys (for example regular high-dose painkillers)

sources.title: ISSN position stand: creatine supplementation (Kreider et al., 2017)

supplements.name: Vitamin D3
supplements.summary: Supports bones and muscles. Low levels are common in India despite the sun.

evidence.use: Correcting low vitamin D found on a blood test

supplements.typical_dose: 600 to 1,000 IU a day for maintenance; higher amounts only as advised by a doctor
supplements.timing: With a meal that has some fat, which helps absorption.
cautions: More is not better: the upper limit for adults is 4,000 IU a day unless a doctor advises otherwise.
High weekly doses (like 60,000 IU sachets) should be taken only as prescribed.
interactions: Some steroid medicines and seizure medicines lower vitamin D levels
Thiazide diuretics with high doses can raise calcium

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin D fact sheet

supplements.name: Vitamin B12
supplements.summary: Needed for nerves and red blood cells. It comes mainly from animal foods.

evidence.use: Vegetarians and vegans, who get little B12 from food
Correcting low B12 found on a blood test

supplements.typical_dose: Small daily amounts (for example 2.4 to 25 mcg) or as advised by a doctor
cautions: If a test shows very low B12, your doctor may suggest a different form or injections.
interactions: Metformin and acid-reducing medicines (PPIs) can lower B12 over time

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin B12 fact sheet

supplements.name: Omega-3 (fish or algae oil)
supplements.summary: EPA and DHA fats found in oily fish; algae oil is the vegetarian source.

evidence.use: Lowering high triglycerides (higher doses, with a doctor)
General heart health for people who don't eat fish

supplements.typical_dose: 250 to 500 mg EPA plus DHA a day
supplements.timing: With a meal, which also reduces fishy aftertaste.
cautions: Fish oil isn't vegetarian; algae oil is.
Higher doses can slightly increase bleeding risk.
interactions: Blood thinners such as warfarin or clopidogrel: check with your doctor first

sources.title: NIH ODS: Omega-3 Fatty Acids fact sheet

supplements.name: Iron
supplements.summary: Needed to make haemoglobin. Only worth taking when a test shows you need it.

evidence.use: Correcting iron deficiency found on a blood test

supplements.typical_dose: Only as advised by a doctor after a blood test
supplements.timing: Away from tea, coffee and calcium; vitamin C helps absorption.
cautions: Too much iron is harmful. Don't take it without a test showing low iron or ferritin.
Can cause constipation or stomach upset.
Keep away from children: iron overdose is dangerous for them.
interactions: Thyroid medicine (levothyroxine): take at least 4 hours apart
Calcium and antacids reduce iron absorption

supplements.name: Magnesium
supplements.summary: A mineral for muscles and nerves, found in nuts, seeds, whole grains and greens.
supplements.typical_dose: 100 to 350 mg a day from supplements (the adult upper limit for supplements is 350 mg)
cautions: Higher doses can cause loose stools.
Not advised with kidney disease unless your doctor agrees.
interactions: Some antibiotics and osteoporosis medicines: take a few hours apart
Thyroid medicine: take at least 4 hours apart

supplements.name: Calcium
supplements.summary: For bones; useful mainly when your diet has little dairy or other calcium-rich food.

evidence.use: Filling a dietary gap, especially with little dairy

supplements.typical_dose: 500 mg or less at a time; total intake from food and supplements around 1,000 mg a day
supplements.timing: With food, split across the day if more than 500 mg.
cautions: Food sources are preferred; very high supplement intake may raise kidney stone risk.
interactions: Thyroid medicine and iron: take at least 4 hours apart

supplements.name: Multivitamin
supplements.summary: A broad backup for small gaps in the diet. It doesn't replace good food.
supplements.typical_dose: One tablet a day as on the label
cautions: Check the label so you don't double up with other supplements (for example vitamin D or iron).
interactions: Contains minerals that should be taken 4 hours apart from thyroid medicine

sources.title: NIH ODS: Multivitamin/mineral Supplements fact sheet

supplements.name: Caffeine
supplements.summary: Improves alertness and endurance; you probably already get some from tea or coffee.
supplements.typical_dose: 3 to 6 mg per kg about an hour before exercise in studies; most adults should stay under 400 mg a day in total
supplements.timing: 30 to 60 minutes before training; avoid within 6 hours of bedtime.
cautions: Count tea, coffee and pre-workout products together.
Can raise blood pressure and heart rate for a while.
During pregnancy, keep caffeine under 200 mg a day.
interactions: Some medicines slow caffeine breakdown (for example certain antibiotics)

sources.title: ISSN position stand: caffeine and exercise performance (Guest et al., 2021)
NIH ODS: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance

supplements.name: Electrolytes
supplements.summary: Sodium and potassium drinks to replace what's lost in heavy sweating.

evidence.use: Long or hot training sessions with heavy sweating

supplements.typical_dose: As on the label, during or after long sweaty sessions
cautions: Most short workouts only need water.
Many products are high in sodium or sugar.
interactions: Blood pressure medicines and potassium-sparing diuretics: check potassium-containing products with your doctor

sources.title: ACSM position stand: Exercise and fluid replacement (Sawka et al., 2007)

supplements.name: Ashwagandha
supplements.summary: An Ayurvedic herb studied for stress and sleep. Evidence is early and safety questions remain.
supplements.typical_dose: Studies mostly used 250 to 600 mg of root extract a day for up to 3 months
cautions: Rare cases of liver injury have been reported.
Not for pregnancy or breastfeeding.
May affect thyroid hormone levels.
Herbal products vary a lot in quality.
interactions: Diabetes and blood pressure medicines (may add to their effect)
